prompt:
I run a small blog for Tidewater Pantry, a shop that sells preserved lemons and fermented hot sauces. Our latest post is a long read and people say it's tiring on the eyes. Build me the post page so it reads comfortably. Give me one self-contained HTML file with inline CSS, system fonts only and no external assets.

Title: Why we stopped rushing the brine
Byline: Imogen Vasquez-Ruiz, Production lead, 9 min read

Intro: For our first three years we salted lemons on Monday and shipped them on Friday. They sold fine. They also tasted flat, and we knew it.

Section "The week we waited": In March we left a single crate alone for five weeks. The rind softened, the pith lost its bitterness, and the juice turned syrupy and almost floral. We opened the jar at the packing table and nobody said anything for a good ten seconds. Then Teodor asked if we could do that with everything.

Section "What it cost us": Waiting is expensive. Every jar sits on a shelf we pay for, and every week of delay is a week of cash we don't have. We moved from 40 jars a week to 12 while the first long batches matured, and two wholesale accounts quietly left. We lost about $3,800 in the spring quarter.

Section "What changed": By June the long batches were selling out in a day. Reorders from the cafes that stayed were up 31 percent. We now run a rolling calendar, with six crates at different stages, so there is always something ready without ever rushing a jar.

Pull quote: "The brine isn't a step. It's the product."

Closing: If you'd like to taste the difference, the five-week lemons are back in stock on Thursday.
rubric: Body copy is set at a comfortable reading size (roughly 17 to 20px on a desktop screen), not small or dense.
The text column is constrained to a readable line length, roughly 50 to 80 characters per line, rather than stretching across the full viewport.
Line spacing for body paragraphs is open enough to read comfortably (clearly more than tight single spacing) and paragraphs are separated by visible space.
The title, section headings, byline and pull quote form a clear stepped order; spacing above each section heading is larger than the space below it, so each heading belongs to the text after it.
The page renders as a single column with no horizontal scrolling or clipped text and uses only system fonts with no external assets.
Identifies that the 13px body size is too small for sustained reading on this page and recommends a concrete larger size.
Identifies that the line length is far too long when the text fills a 1440px window and recommends a concrete cap on the text column.
Identifies the tight line height and the cramped paragraph and list spacing and gives concrete replacement values.
Points out that the heading sizes are too close to one another and to body text, and that spacing around headings does not group them with the text that follows.
Notes the negative letter-spacing on body text as a cause of crowding and recommends removing it.
Prioritises the fixes and gives specific values rather than only describing the problems; does not drift into changing the typeface or colors.

rubric: The money columns line up so that decimal points and digits stack vertically; amounts are right-aligned or otherwise decimal-aligned, not left-aligned.
Digits in the figure columns are set to equal widths (tabular figures or a monospaced face) so that rows with different digits still align.
Every money value shows two decimals with the currency symbol used consistently, and thousands separators are present; the negative discount is clearly marked.
Column headers sit over their data and share its alignment (numeric headers right-aligned with their numbers, text headers left-aligned).
The Total due is visibly distinct from the other summary rows through size, weight or a rule, without needing a color change, and the totals block lines up with the amount column.
Text and figures are legible at normal size and the page uses only system fonts with no external assets.

Says plainly that the existing setup is already sound and names several specific things that work (for example the reading size, the column width, the line spacing, the heading spacing or the tracked small label).
Leaves the large majority of the existing values unchanged; any edits are few and small, not a rewrite of the stylesheet.
Each change it does make is explained with a concrete reason and shown with values.
Does not respond to "more editorial" by swapping typefaces, adding decorative effects, enlarging everything, or changing colors.
Does not make the text worse, for example by raising body size sharply, tightening the line height or widening the column.

prompt:
We're building a build-log viewer for our CI tool, the pane where developers read the output of a failed job. Lines can be 120 to 200 characters and include stack traces and aligned columns of timings. My teammate wants it to match our blog, so she'd go with A. I think B. Which should we ship?

A:
```css
.log { font: 16px/1.7 system-ui, sans-serif; max-width: 60ch; white-space: normal; }
```
B:
```css
.log { font: 13px/1.45 ui-monospace, Menlo, Consolas, monospace; white-space: pre; overflow-x: auto; }
```
C:
```css
.log { font: 15px/1.6 ui-monospace, Menlo, Consolas, monospace; max-width: 60ch; white-space: pre-wrap; }
```
rubric: Picks B or a close variant of B (monospace, unwrapped or horizontally scrollable) and gives a clear recommendation rather than leaving it open.
Explains that this content needs a monospaced face and preserved spacing because stack traces and timing columns have to line up, which A would destroy.
Explains that a short fixed line length and wrapping, which suit prose, would break long log lines and alignment here and is not a defect to fix.
Rejects A with a reason tied to this content and does not defer to matching the blog for its own sake.
Any suggested tweak is modest and concrete (for example slightly more line height or a size nudge) and does not undo the recommendation.

prompt:
I'm printing a one-page A4 menu for Saltmarsh Kitchen, a 30-seat seafood place. I'll do the layout in a word processor and I don't know how to set the type so it looks like a proper restaurant menu and not a spreadsheet. How should I set it? Content:

STARTERS: Oyster of the day, shallot vinegar 4.5 each. Smoked mackerel pate, pickled cucumber, rye toast 9. Crab and fennel salad 12.5.
MAINS: Whole grilled bream, salsa verde, new potatoes 24. Mussels in cider and cream, chips 18. Cauliflower steak, almond romesco 17. Fish pie, peas 19.5.
PUDDINGS: Burnt honey tart 8. Rhubarb trifle 7.5. Cheese plate 11.
Also a short line at the bottom: Please tell us about allergies before ordering. A discretionary 12.5% service charge is added to tables of six or more.
rubric: Gives concrete sizes in points (or equivalent) for each level: restaurant name or title, section headings, dish names, descriptions, and the footer line.
Keeps the number of distinct type levels small (about 3 to 5) and makes the hierarchy readable by size, weight or case rather than many styles.
Specifies how prices are placed and aligned consistently, such as a common right edge or decimal alignment, with a stated treatment for numbers like 4.5, 9 and 24 so they look uniform.
Sets dish names apart from their descriptions (for example by weight or size) and puts more space between sections than between items.
If it uses capitals for section labels, it says to add letterspacing to them; it keeps the allergy and service-charge line small but still legible.
Avoids justified text and a long list of fonts or effects.

prompt: The live attendee counter on our event page wiggles sideways every time the number ticks over, and the text next to it shifts. It's a plain span in a normal sans-serif font. Why does that happen and how do I stop it? Keep it under 80 words please.
rubric: Explains that the digits in this font have different widths, so the counter's total width changes as the digits change.
Gives a concrete fix that works, such as the tabular-figures CSS setting or a monospaced face, or reserving a fixed width for the number.
The answer is 80 words or fewer.
Stays on the question without extra topics such as a general typography lecture or a redesign of the page.

prompt:
Can you clean up the typography in this blurb for our shop page? Keep the wording exactly as it is.

Thanks for stopping by Harlow & Finch -- we've been making oak shelves since 1998, all by hand. Our "Pocket" shelf is 6' x 2", ships in 3-5 days, and costs $48-$60. It's the one our customers call 'the keeper'. Don't take our word for it -- ask a neighbor.
rubric: Uses typographic (curly) apostrophes and double quotation marks, including around "Pocket" and the nested single quotation marks around the keeper.
Turns the 3-5 and $48-$60 ranges into en dashes and the double hyphens into proper dashes consistently.
Keeps the foot and inch marks in 6' x 2" as straight or prime marks and does not turn them into curly quotation marks; replacing the x with a multiplication sign is acceptable.
Does not change any words, numbers, punctuation order or meaning beyond the typographic characters.
Presents the cleaned-up text clearly and notes briefly which kinds of characters it changed, without a long explanation.

prompt:
Build a status page for Quillbase, our hosted notes API, with a dark theme because our users are developers who sit in dark editors all day. Give me one self-contained HTML file with inline CSS, system fonts only and no external assets.

Content: heading "Quillbase status"; a one-line summary "All systems operational" with the note "Last checked 4 minutes ago"; a list of components with 30-day uptime: API 99.98%, Sync service 99.91%, Web editor 99.99%, Webhooks 99.62%, Search 100%; a past-incidents section with two entries. Incident one, 21 September, "Webhook delays": "Deliveries were delayed by up to 40 minutes between 08:10 and 09:05 UTC while we rebalanced a queue. All delayed events were delivered. We have added an alert for queue depth." Incident two, 6 September, "Sync lag in EU region": "Changes took up to 12 seconds to appear on a second device for about 25 minutes. We rolled back a deployment and the lag cleared."
rubric: Body text is easy to read on the dark background: neither pure white on pure black glare nor dim gray that is hard to read, with a comfortable size (about 16px or larger) and clear line spacing.
Text carries at least three clearly distinct levels (primary text, secondary text, labels or metadata) that remain legible on the dark background.
The uptime percentages align as a column (equal-width figures, consistent decimals or alignment) so they can be compared at a glance.
The incident paragraphs are set at a comfortable line length and size, with the date, title and body clearly separated.
The page has no horizontal scrolling, uses only system fonts and no external assets, and does not rely on light-weight thin text that thins out on dark.
